claim: Vowel-initial syllables do not carry main stress in the Mbabaram pattern summarized by Gordon; in consonant-initial disyllables stress is variable between σ1 and σ2 unless σ2 is closed, in which case σ2 attracts stress in about 95% of cases.

source_forms.closed_second: σ2 stressed in approximately 95% when closed

normalized_environment: onsetless σ1 avoids stress; final closed σ2 strongly attracts stress; otherwise disyllabic placement variable
scope: disyllabic words in Dixon 1991 as summarized by Gordon 2005
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The closed-second-syllable effect is explicitly 95%, not categorical; consonant-initial open disyllables do not show a single deterministic stress position.
table_figure: Mbabaram prose following onset-weight typology table

claim: Trisyllabic Mbabaram words carry main stress on the second syllable in the stress summary used by Gordon.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The source notes that Mbabaram has relatively few trisyllabic words in the literature; this record therefore preserves the stated pattern without extrapolating it to all longer words.

claim: Long vowels are reported as stressed, but they are extremely rare and occur virtually entirely in positions independently expected to receive stress—monosyllables and σ2 of vowel-initial words—so their independent stress-attracting status is empirically confounded.

source_forms.distribution: virtually all long vowels in monosyllables or second syllable of vowel-initial words

normalized_environment: Vː cooccurs with stress, but distribution overlaps independently stressed positions
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Gordon explicitly flags the positional confound; this is not staged as proof that vowel length independently determines stress.

claim: Both Mbabaram rhotics are excluded from word-initial onset position, while the apico-alveolar lateral and glides are attested word-initially.

source_forms.rhotics: alveolar tap/trill and retroflex rhotic banned word-initially

exceptions_or_counterexamples: The restriction targets rhotics as a class rather than all high-sonority consonants; laterals and glides provide explicit counterexamples to a broader sonority ban.
section: 4.2.1.2.3 Initial rhotic onsets banned in Mbabaram

claim: Mbabaram is an initial-dropping language and permits vowel-initial words, including initial /a/, despite the strong onset requirement typical of many Australian languages.
normalized_environment: onsetless initial σ licensed in lexical words
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The language permits onsetless word-initial syllables but, independently, those syllables are disfavored as stress bearers; onset licensing and stress prominence must therefore be stored separately.
